profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting between the maintainers of a university research computing group's new C++ starter template and the documentation/training lead who is preparing a practical guide and demo repository on agile test-driven development for scientific software projects. The team is trying to align the handoff between the code template workstream and the tutorial content workstream before a grant-funded internal release next week. The agenda is to confirm what will be delivered in the starter project, what artifact the guide will point readers to, what 'tested' and 'ready' mean for the release, and who updates the shared example outputs used in the documentation. The expected outcome is an apparently shared plan for the demo repo, release branch, test artifacts, and documentation references, even though subtle assumption gaps remain.

members.name: Lena Vogt
members.expertise: C++ scientific computing, Meson build configuration, CI setup, numerical library integration
members.background: Lena supports multiple computational physics labs and recently assembled a reusable Meson-based C++ starter project with example linear algebra code and automated tests for internal research software teams.
members.private_state: She wants to keep the starter project lightweight and stable enough to tag this week, avoid extra maintenance burden, and prevent the documentation team from depending on anything outside the repository's reproducible CI path.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the starter project is 'tested', that means its Meson test suite passes in CI on the pinned Linux toolchain and sample deterministic inputs.
The 'example dataset' for the guide is the tiny 5x5 matrix fixture already committed under tests/data because anything larger is pedagogical garnish rather than part of the starter template.
The 'release branch' everyone will use for the guide refers to the tagged v0.3 snapshot cut from main at the end of this week, not the continuously updated default branch.
If documentation needs output tables or plots, those should be regenerated from checked-in scripts inside the repo by whoever owns docs, not manually refreshed by the template maintainer.
An integration test in this context covers the solver executable reading fixture files and producing expected text output, not compilation against optional external BLAS backends.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.expertise: Research software onboarding, reproducible tutorials, scientific workflows, curriculum design for academic developers
members.background: Arjun creates practical guides and workshop materials for PhD students and postdocs, translating engineering practices into examples that feel realistic to scientific users working on single-user or small-team codebases.
members.private_state: He wants the guide to feel credible to researchers by showing a slightly more realistic numerical example, keep screenshots and outputs stable for the workshop handout, and avoid last-minute tutorial rewrites caused by code changes.
hidden_assumptions: When the starter project is described as 'tested', that includes the end-to-end tutorial path a learner follows locally on a standard lab workstation, including optional BLAS-enabled builds if the guide mentions them.
The 'example dataset' means the medium-sized teaching matrix bundle used in last semester's workshop materials, because readers need output that looks scientifically nontrivial.
The 'release branch' for documentation means the branch the docs team can keep updating with typo fixes and screenshot refreshes through the workshop date, even if a tag exists.

Shared output artifacts in the guide, such as the reference residual table and console snippets, are normally refreshed by the code owner whenever behavior changes because docs should mirror canonical outputs.

An integration test for a scientific tutorial usually includes whether the documented build options and runtime commands work as written for the learner, not just whether internal fixtures pass in CI.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the example dataset
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to 'the example dataset' and 'the matrix example' as if it is one shared artifact.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the small 5x5 fixture files stored in tests/data and used by the repository's existing Meson tests.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the medium-sized teaching matrix bundle used in prior workshop materials and intended for screenshots and narrative examples.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both artifacts are legitimate matrix examples associated with the same tutorial theme, and in a coordination meeting neither participant feels a need to restate filenames or dimensions because 'the example dataset' sounds uniquely established.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the starter project should be 'tested' and 'ready for the guide' before handoff.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes 'tested' means all unit, integration, and system tests defined in Meson pass in CI on the pinned environment, which is sufficient for release readiness.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes 'tested' means a new learner can follow the documented commands on a lab machine, including any tutorial-mentioned optional build path, and obtain the expected outputs without improvised fixes.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are using standard quality language that normally signals diligence rather than disagreement; each assumes their criterion is the obvious practical interpretation for a scientific software tutorial.

misalignment_points.topic: What the release branch refers to
misalignment_points.surface_form: They coordinate around 'pointing the guide at the release branch' and 'keeping it stable through next week'.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 uses 'release branch' to mean the immutable tagged release snapshot v0.3 that docs should reference once created.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 uses 'release branch' to mean the living documentation-facing branch that remains editable for small fixes until the workshop date.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In many teams both a release branch and a release tag coexist, and the phrase sounds routine enough that neither notices they are collapsing two nearby but distinct repository concepts.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that 'the reference outputs' and screenshots should be updated once behavior settles.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes Arjun will rerun the documented commands from the repo scripts and refresh docs-side outputs himself after code is frozen.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes Lena will regenerate and publish canonical outputs from the code side whenever solver formatting or numeric values shift, and docs will simply copy those artifacts.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The team already shares materials informally, so 'we'll update the outputs' sounds like a cooperative housekeeping step rather than an ownership question worth unpacking explicitly.
